canonical.title: Which Linux to switch to in 2026: a decision framework for a .NET developer leaving Windows

children.title: The 2026 Linux distro landscape: what actually differs between the families
children.summary: There are only five real distro families, and for a Windows developer moving to Linux in 2026 the honest shortlist is Fedora Workstation, Ubuntu LTS, Linux Mint, Bluefin/Aurora, and openSUSE Tumbleweed — everything else is a variation, a server OS, or a hobby.

children.title: Stable, rolling, or atomic: picking a release model for your first Linux daily driver
children.summary: Start on a 6-month fixed release (Fedora Workstation) or an atomic Fedora image (Bluefin DX); avoid pure rolling and avoid Debian stable — and here is the evidence for each release model's breakage, rollback, and software-age tradeoffs.

children.title: Toolchain fit: which Linux distro costs least setup work for .NET 10 + TypeScript + Docker in 2026
children.summary: For a .NET 10 + TypeScript + Docker workstation in 2026, Ubuntu 26.04 LTS and Fedora 44 tie on setup effort and every other family costs you at least one hand-configured vendor repo.

children.title: Picking a Linux desktop in 2026: the Windows 11 switcher's decision guide
children.summary: KDE Plasma is the lowest-friction landing spot for a Windows 11 developer in 2026; X11 sessions die this year, so the real choice is which Wayland compositor's rough edges you can live with.

children.title: Hardware and driver reality in 2026: only three things should decide your distro
children.summary: In 2026 only three hardware classes still force a distro choice — NVIDIA, very new silicon, and Secure-Boot dual-boot; everything else is a live-USB check away.

children.title: Windows to Linux in 2026: what crosses over, what doesn't, and how to stage the switch
children.summary: Almost everything a .NET developer does crosses to Linux in 2026 — the four things that don't are desktop Office with VBA, a native Outlook with working calendar, WPF/WinForms designers, and Windows-only compliance tooling; keep a Windows partition for those and stage the switch through live USB and dual-boot before committing.

children.title: Linux upkeep in 2026: support windows, upgrade pain, and monthly chores ranked
children.summary: Ranked by ongoing upkeep for a learning-level Linux user: atomic Fedora and Ubuntu/Mint LTS are near-zero chore; Fedora Workstation costs one upgrade a year; Arch costs a reading habit you cannot skip.

children.title: Gaming and media on Linux in 2026: singleplayer is solved, anti-cheat and DRM streaming are not
children.summary: Roughly 90% of Windows Steam titles launch under Proton; the two real losses are kernel anti-cheat multiplayer (Call of Duty, Valorant, Battlefield 6) and browser DRM streaming above 720p SDR.

sources.title: fedoramagazine.org
sources.claim: Fedora Linux 44 shipped 28 April 2026 with kernel 6.19, GNOME 50, Plasma 6.6, and Atomic Desktop variants alongside the traditional editions.

sources.title: documentation.ubuntu.com
sources.claim: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS was released 23 April 2026 with five years of security updates through April 2031.

sources.title: docs.projectbluefin.io
sources.claim: Bluefin checks for updates every six hours and applies them at reboot; the stable stream publishes weekly images with a kernel gated about two weeks behind Fedora; rollback uses bootc status / bootc switch to dated tags; local package layering is locked off by default via LockLayering and warned to require manual maintenance and longer updates.

sources.title: www.omgubuntu.co.uk
sources.claim: Linux Mint 23 (due end of 2026) fully supports both X11 and Wayland; Mint has not committed to making Wayland the default.

sources.title: www.phoronix.com
sources.claim: More than 1,500 AUR packages were affected; Arch published a list of 1,579 compromised packages and believed the incident contained.

sources.title: archlinux.org
sources.claim: Arch publishes breaking-change and manual-intervention notices that must be read before upgrading; only 4 news items appeared in the first seven months of 2026.

sources.title: kde.org
sources.claim: Plasma 6.7 (16 June 2026) adds per-screen virtual desktops, simultaneous ICC colour management plus HDR, and performance/power improvements.

sources.title: www.xda-developers.com
sources.claim: GNOME 50 removed the X11 session entirely (about 27,540 lines cut from Mutter); you cannot log into an X11 GNOME session even with Xorg installed, though X11 apps still run under XWayland.

sources.title: linuxiac.com
sources.claim: Plasma 6.8 (expected 14 Oct 2026) drops the dedicated X11 session; Plasma 6.7 is the last with one, and the X11 session is maintained only until early 2027.

sources.title: fedoramagazine.org
sources.claim: Fedora KDE 44 ships Plasma 6.6.4 along with the new Plasma Setup and Plasma Keyboard components.

sources.title: github.com
sources.claim: Aurora is Universal Blue's KDE Plasma image, the atomic counterpart to Bluefin.

sources.title: sysguides.com
sources.claim: Fedora's default installer does not create a btrfs layout suited to snapshot management, and automatic pre/post snapshots require manually installing snapper plus the DNF5 actions plugin and grub-btrfs.

sources.title: linux.slashdot.org
sources.claim: Dropbox on Linux supports only unencrypted ext4 for the sync folder because it relies on extended attributes; ext4 inside a LUKS volume is still fine, but ext4's own file-based encryption is not.

sources.title: docs.bazzite.gg
sources.claim: Atomic Fedora derivatives stage each update as a new deployment, always keep a rollback deployment, and move major version via rpm-ostree rebase.

sources.title: discussion.fedoraproject.org
sources.claim: A May 2026 Fedora Kinoite 44 thread shows an update blocked by an NVIDIA akmod dependency conflict during a kernel bump.

sources.title: areweanticheatyet.com
sources.claim: Of games using anti-cheat: 17% supported, 24% running, 55% broken, 4% denied; Fortnite, Valorant, Apex Legends and Rainbow Six Siege are in the Denied bucket.

sources.title: www.xda-developers.com
sources.claim: Linux browsers are limited to Widevine L3 software DRM, capping Netflix/Prime/HBO at SD-720p SDR with no HDR; HDR gaming is Wayland-only and AMD/NVIDIA-only, Intel incomplete.

sources.title: learn.microsoft.com
sources.claim: Microsoft 365 desktop apps are supported only on Windows and macOS; the web version in a browser is the supported route on Linux.

sources.title: eid.belgium.be
sources.claim: The Belgian eID cannot be used with Snap or Flatpak software because sandbox confinement blocks the PKCS#11 module; a natively packaged browser is required.

sources.title: linuxlap.com
sources.claim: Microsoft's UEFI CA 2011 certificate expired 27 June 2026; major distros ship dual-signed shims so Secure Boot can stay enabled; BitLocker recovery is triggered by boot/ESP changes.

sources.title: www.phoronix.com
sources.claim: New Intel (Xe3P_LPG, Nova Lake) and AMD (DCN 4.2) GPU enablement lands per kernel release, so kernel recency governs support for new silicon.

sources.title: github.com
sources.claim: Bluefin is Universal Blue's GNOME workstation image, positioned as a reliability-focused Linux workstation.

sources.title: docs.projectbluefin.io
sources.claim: Bluefin positions itself as not a distribution, with the user's relationship being with Flathub, Homebrew and their own containers rather than a host package manager.

sources.title: docs.projectbluefin.io
sources.claim: Bluefin's developer image ships docker-ce with the Compose and Buildx plugins plus Podman tooling and VS Code with Dev Containers preconfigured.

sources.title: docs.projectbluefin.io
sources.claim: Bluefin prompts for Universal Blue MOK key enrolment at first boot so signed NVIDIA/ZFS kernel modules load under Secure Boot.

sources.title: fedoraproject.org
sources.claim: Fedora ships five Atomic Desktop variants — Silverblue (GNOME), Kinoite (KDE), Sway, Budgie and COSMIC — with an image-based, versioned base system.

sources.title: fedoraproject.org
sources.claim: Each Fedora release is supported for about 13 months — until roughly one month after the release of version X+2 — allowing users to skip a release.

sources.title: fedoraproject.org
sources.claim: Fedora installs the proprietary NVIDIA driver under Secure Boot by generating a local key with mokutil and prompting the user to enrol it on reboot.

sources.title: ubuntu.com
sources.claim: Ubuntu LTS gets 5 years standard security maintenance, 10 years with Ubuntu Pro ESM, 15 years with the Legacy add-on; interim releases get 9 months.

sources.title: ubuntu.com
sources.claim: Ubuntu LTS offers a GA kernel frozen at release and an HWE stack that provides newer kernel and display support on a rolling basis, with desktop installs defaulting to HWE.

sources.title: github.com
sources.claim: Cinnamon's upstream development home is the Linux Mint project itself.

sources.title: www.omgubuntu.co.uk
sources.claim: Linux Mint 22.3 'Zena' (January 2026) is based on Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS with Cinnamon 6.6 and is supported to April 2029.

sources.title: www.phoronix.com
sources.claim: Linux Mint 23 is being built on the Ubuntu 26.04 LTS base with the Linux 7.0 kernel and Wayland work.

sources.title: doc.opensuse.org
sources.claim: openSUSE Tumbleweed publishes snapshots several times a week, gated by openQA testing; the update command is zypper dup, and rollback is done by booting a read-only snapshot from GRUB2 then running snapper rollback.

sources.title: doc.opensuse.org
sources.claim: openSUSE integrates snapper with btrfs as a first-class, default-enabled helper for reverting the system to a previous state.

sources.title: news.opensuse.org
sources.claim: openSUSE Leap 15.6 reached EOL at the end of April 2026 and moving to Leap 16 requires a dedicated migration tool.

sources.title: www.debian.org
sources.claim: Debian 13 'trixie' is current stable at point release 13.6 (11 July 2026); testing is 'forky'; each stable gets three years of full support plus two years of LTS.

sources.title: archlinux.org
sources.claim: On 12 June 2026 Arch announced an active AUR incident of malicious package adoptions and updates, telling users to review every PKGBUILD and install-script change.

sources.title: release.gnome.org
sources.claim: GNOME 50 enables fractional scaling and VRR by default, improves NVIDIA performance, and gives Remote Desktop Vulkan/VA-API acceleration, HiDPI-aware scaling, camera redirection and Kerberos auth.

sources.title: kde.org
sources.claim: Plasma 6.6 shipped 17 February 2026 with new first-party modules (plasma-login-manager, plasma-keyboard, plasma-setup), improved cross-app activation on Wayland and theme/global-theme features.

sources.title: github.com
sources.claim: KDE is effectively the only desktop with a working GlobalShortcuts portal backend; GNOME 50 has none functional and xdg-desktop-portal-wlr ships no implementation.

sources.title: discourse.gnome.org
sources.claim: GNOME extension review runs through a single reviewer; in spring 2026 the queue reached nearly 500 pending submissions, many just metadata bumps for GNOME 50 compatibility.

sources.title: www.tecmint.com
sources.claim: Best-supported KDE homes include Kubuntu (LTS cadence), Fedora KDE Spin (official flagship edition, near-vanilla Plasma), KDE neon (newest Plasma, by the KDE team, on Ubuntu LTS), openSUSE Tumbleweed and EndeavourOS.

sources.claim: Canonical now owns .NET on Ubuntu; Ubuntu 26.04 has .NET 10 in the built-in feed and 9.0/8.0 only via the dotnet/backports PPA, and Canonical SDKs are always in the .1xx feature band.
